qs.e: Autosomal recessive. Gaucher cells = lipid-laden macrophages with "crumpled tissue paper" cytoplasm. Affects liver, spleen (massive), bone marrow. Type 1 (non-neuronopathic) = most common, no CNS involvement. Treatment: enzyme replacement therapy (imiglucerase).

exam: A 12‑year‑old with massive splenomegaly, anemia and bone pain – what is your next diagnostic step? — Order glucocerebrosidase activity assay; if unavailable, send dried blood spot to reference lab.
How does type III Gaucher differ from type I in presentation? — Presence of neurologic signs (oculomotor palsy, seizures) distinguishes type III.

A patient on ERT develops worsening bone pain – what should you consider? — Assess for avascular necrosis or inadequate bone penetration; consider adding bisphosphonate after ruling out renal disease.
Why is it unsafe to give high‑dose steroids in a Gaucher patient with severe thrombocytopenia? — Steroids increase bleeding risk and can worsen infection in already immunocompromised patients.

In a malaria‑endemic area, a child presents with splenomegaly and anemia – how do you differentiate malaria from Gaucher disease? — Look for chronicity, bone pain, and Gaucher cells on smear; malaria shows parasites on thick smear.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for a Gaucher patient? — Sudden severe abdominal pain suggesting splenic rupture.
Explain why substrate reduction therapy may be chosen over ERT in a low‑resource setting. — Oral agents avoid the need for intravenous infusions and cold‑chain storage.
What are the key components of long‑term follow‑up for a patient on ERT? — Serial CBC, organ size assessment, bone pain monitoring, and annual imaging if possible.
ai.title: Gaucher Disease
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Gaucher disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by glucocerebrosidase deficiency, leading to glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages. It presents with organomegaly, cytopenias, bone disease, and can be life‑threatening if untreated.

b: Enzyme assay < 15% normal activity confirms disease
Genetic testing identifies pathogenic GBA mutations
sections.p: A lysosomal storage disease due to deficient glucocerebrosidase (GBA gene). Diagnosis rests on low enzyme activity in leukocytes or dried blood spot and confirmation by genetic testing when available.

t.b: Is the enzyme deficient? – <15% of normal confirms Gaucher disease

t.a: Dried blood spot assay (if lab unavailable, send to reference centre)
t.b: Screening test when full enzyme assay not possible – low activity suggests disease
Which mutation is present? – guides prognosis and eligibility for enzyme replacement

b: Mild: splenomegaly <5 cm, platelets >100 ×10⁹/L, no bone crisis
Moderate: splenomegaly 5–10 cm, platelets 50‑100 ×10⁹/L, early bone pain
Severe: splenomegaly >10 cm, platelets <50 ×10⁹/L, avascular necrosis or fractures
sections.p: Severity is graded by the GD Severity Scoring System (GD‑SDS) incorporating spleen size, platelet count, hemoglobin, and bone involvement.

b: GBA gene loss‑of‑function mutations (most common)
Concurrent HIV or TB causing splenomegaly
Malaria‑related hemolysis that mimics cytopenias
sections.p: Autosomal recessive GBA mutations are the primary cause. In low‑resource settings, co‑existing infections can worsen cytopenias and organomegaly.

b: Massive, non‑tender splenomegaly
Fatigue, pallor, easy bruising (low hemoglobin/platelets)
Bone pain, Erlenmeyer flask deformity on X‑ray
Type II/III: oculomotor palsy, seizures, developmental delay
sections.p: Patients often present with a triad: splenomegaly, anemia or thrombocytopenia, and bone pain. Neurologic involvement distinguishes type II/III forms.
Focus on tests that are feasible in low‑resource hospitals; use clinical clues when advanced imaging is unavailable.

t.b: Is the spleen enlarged? – Confirms organomegaly, assesses liver size
Are cytopenias present? – Anemia <10 g/dL, platelets <150 ×10⁹/L support diagnosis
Are Gaucher cells visible? – Crumpled tissue‑paper macrophages are suggestive
Is there bone remodeling? – Erlenmeyer flask deformity or osteopenia indicates skeletal disease
Are co‑infections present? – Guides supportive management

b: Progressive cytopenias leading to severe infection or bleeding
Avascular necrosis of femur or humerus
Pulmonary hypertension from infiltrative disease
Neurologic decline in type II/III
sections.p: Complications can be fatal if not recognised early.

b: Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with imiglucerase or velaglucerase – restores glucocerebrosidase activity
Substrate reduction therapy (eliglustat) if ERT unavailable and patient can tolerate oral meds
Blood transfusion for severe anemia, platelet transfusion for bleeding
Bisphosphonates for bone pain only after ruling out renal impairment
Treat HIV/TB/malaria aggressively – they worsen cytopenias
sections.p: Treat the enzyme deficiency, manage complications, and address co‑existing infections.

b: Every 6‑12 months: CBC, spleen size (clinical or ultrasound), bone pain assessment
Annual MRI of liver/spleen if resources allow – tracks organ infiltration
Genetic counselling for families; carrier testing for siblings
Splenic sequestration in sickle cell disease
Visceral leishmaniasis (kala‑azar)
Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis
sections.p: Conditions that also cause splenomegaly and cytopenias.

b: Normal glucocerebrosidase activity in heterozygotes – does not rule out disease in symptomatic patients
Mild anemia may be attributed to malaria, delaying diagnosis
sections.p: Some laboratory findings may be normal early in disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid neurological decline in a known Gaucher patient
